491.title: Va'etchanan: the right and the good (Deuteronomy 6:18)
491.hook: do "that which is right and good"; the rabbis read it as going beyond the letter of the law
491.howItsDone: In Jewish ethics and law, acting lifnim mishurat hadin, beyond the letter of the law, is praised as the way of the pious, and some later authorities hold that a court may in certain cases press people to act this way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Va'etchanan and the four places the Shema's words travel. Your line was at home and on the way. Today, the portion's last stop: a phrase that goes past the rules.

Porters are carrying a barrel of wine for a rabbi named Rabbah bar bar Chanan, and they drop it. The barrel breaks. The wine runs into the dirt. By the rules of the time, workers who broke what they carried could be held liable, so the rabbi takes their cloaks as security. The porters go to Rav and complain. The story is in the Talmud, and it's an uncomfortable one, because the rabbi with the broken barrel isn't exactly wrong. Today's phrase is what Rav tells him.
screen: `A BARREL OF WINE IN THE DIRT.` → `HE TAKES THEIR CLOAKS.` → `THEY GO TO RAV.`

segments.voice: Rav says: give them back their cloaks. Is that the law? the rabbi asks. Rav answers with a verse from Proverbs about walking in the way of good people. So he gives the cloaks back. Then the porters say: we're poor, we worked all day, we're hungry, and we have nothing. Rav says: pay them their wages. Is that the law? Yes, Rav says, and quotes the rest of the verse, about keeping the paths of the righteous. The story doesn't use the name, but later teachers reach for it to explain a phrase the Talmud uses elsewhere: lifnim mishurat hadin. Literally, inside the line of the law. Not breaking the law. Standing back from the edge of it, where you could legally stand, and choosing to give more. Where does it come from? One root is today's verse from Va'etchanan: "And thou shalt do that which is right and good in the sight of the LORD." The medieval teacher Nachmanides, the Ramban, explains it like this. The Torah can't list every situation between neighbors and business partners and friends. So after all the specific rules, it adds a general one. Do the right and the good. Compromise. Give way. Go further than the line. The Talmud makes the same point darkly elsewhere: it says Jerusalem was destroyed because people judged strictly by the letter of the law and never went beyond it. A society can follow every rule and still be hard.

Lifnim. Inside: short for lifnim mishurat hadin, inside the line of the law, choosing to give more than the law requires because it's right and good.
Your line: beyond the letter. The right and the good asks more than any list of rules. Rest well.

492.title: Eikev: not by bread only (Deuteronomy 8:3)
492.hook: "man doth not live by bread only", the lesson of the manna
492.howItsDone: Eikev is read in synagogues in late summer, and on the Sabbath two loaves are set on the table, a custom tied to the double portion of manna that fell before the Sabbath.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lifnim: inside the line of the law, the right and the good. Your line was beyond the letter. Today a new portion, Eikev, and a sentence people quote without knowing its home.

Man does not live by bread alone. It gets said about jobs that pay well and feel empty, about art, about weekends. It's often taken for an old proverb, or for a line from the Gospels, where Jesus quotes it in the wilderness. But it's a quotation there too. Its home is here, in Moses' farewell, and it isn't about bread in general. It's about one very specific food that fell from the sky every morning for forty years.
screen: `NOT BY BREAD ALONE.` → `A LINE PEOPLE QUOTE.` → `ITS HOME IS HERE.`

segments.voice: First the portion's name. Eikev means because, from its opening: because you listen to these laws, blessing will follow. But eikev is also the Hebrew word for heel, the same root as Jacob, who came out holding his brother's heel. Rashi plays on it: eikev points to the small commandments people tend to trample under their heels, the ones that seem minor. Then Moses turns back to the wilderness. In the old Jewish translation: "And He afflicted thee, and suffered thee to hunger, and fed thee with manna, which thou knewest not, neither did thy fathers know; that He might make thee know that man doth not live by bread only, but by every thing that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD doth man live." Hear the order. Hunger first, then a food no one recognized. Manna couldn't be stored; it spoiled overnight, except for the Sabbath portion. You couldn't stockpile it or own it. Every morning you depended again. And the point, Moses says, was a lesson: bread is real, people need it, but life doesn't come only from what you can grow or buy or keep. In his telling, it also comes from somewhere no one controls. He adds a detail to make it vivid: "Thy raiment waxed not old upon thee, neither did thy foot swell, these forty years." Forty years of walking, and their feet held. Not by bread only, Moses says. Not bread never, either. Bread, and more than bread.

segments.voice: Notice your body, hungry, full or somewhere between: that's the bread part, and it's real. Then ask what you've been living on lately besides food, and what truly nourishes you that you've let go thin: a walk, an old friend, a page of something beautiful, a few minutes of quiet. Name one, and hold it the way you'd hold warm bread.
Eikev. Because, and also heel. The name of the portion, from its opening word: because you listen.
Your line: not by bread alone. The manna came one morning at a time. See you tomorrow.

493.title: Eikev: not my hand alone (Deuteronomy 8:17–18)
493.hook: beware saying "my power and the might of my hand" earned this
493.howItsDone: Jews say birkat hamazon, the grace after meals, after eating bread, based on Deuteronomy 8:10, and some teachers pair it with the warning a few verses later against saying my power and the might of my hand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eikev and the manna, a food no one could store. Your line was not by bread alone. Today, what happens once the bread is plentiful.

A founder at a podcast microphone tells the success story. I started in a garage. I worked eighteen-hour days. Nobody believed in me. It's often true. But the parents who covered rent, the teacher who noticed, the lucky timing, the country with roads and courts, the health that held: they often get edited out. Not out of malice. Success tends to tell itself in the first person. Moses saw this coming for a people about to move from tents into houses. In the middle of Eikev he warns them about one sentence they'll be tempted to say.
screen: `I STARTED IN A GARAGE.` → `THE EDITED-OUT HELP.` → `ONE SENTENCE TO WATCH FOR.`

segments.voice: The chapter starts with gratitude. In the old Jewish translation: "And thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God for the good land which He hath given thee." That verse is the root of the Jewish grace after meals, birkat hamazon. You eat, you're full, you bless. Then, right away, the warning. When you've eaten and are full, Moses says, and built fine houses, and your herds and silver and gold have multiplied, watch out that your heart doesn't lift itself up and forget. And the sentence: "and thou say in thy heart: 'My power and the might of my hand hath gotten me this wealth.'" In Hebrew, kochi v'otzem yadi. My strength, and the might of my hand. Then the answer: "But thou shalt remember the LORD thy God, for it is He that giveth thee power to get wealth." Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say you did nothing, or that work is pointless. Your hand was real. It says the power in the hand came from somewhere. Strength, health, wits, the land itself: in the verse's telling, given. The danger isn't wealth. It's the sentence, said in your heart, that erases everyone and everything that made the wealth possible. And notice the timing. Not in hunger. The warning comes when you're full. The same full stomach that leads to a blessing can lead to forgetting, and Moses puts the two side by side, a few verses apart.

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're proud of, and tell its story to yourself in one sentence, the way you would at a party. Now tell it again, slowly, and let the hidden helpers in: who paid, taught, waited, believed you, and what luck you had. Let your thanks rest on one of them.
Eikev. Because, and heel. The portion where Moses warns a full people about the sentence my hand did this.
Your line: not my hand alone. The hand was real, and so were the helpers. Day four hundred ninety-three, done.

494.title: Eikev: what is asked (Deuteronomy 10:12)
494.hook: what does God require but to revere, walk in God's ways, love and serve
494.howItsDone: Following Rabbi Meir's reading of this verse, many observant Jews aim to say a hundred blessings each day, across the morning blessings, the prayer services and the blessings over food.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eikev's warning for full days: my power and the might of my hand. Your line was not my hand alone. Today, a question with a short answer.

By this point in his farewell, Moses has given his people a lot: the wilderness story retold, the Ten Commandments again, the Shema, warning after warning about forgetting. And the long run of laws, courts, kings, food and festivals is still ahead. Standing in that crowd, you might feel the weight of it pressing down. How could anyone carry all of this? Then, in the middle of Eikev, Moses stops, takes a breath, and asks the question for them, in the plainest words in the book. So what, exactly, is being asked of you?
screen: `SO MUCH SAID, MORE TO COME.` → `HOW COULD ANYONE CARRY THIS?` → `MOSES ASKS THE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "And now, Israel, what doth the LORD thy God require of thee, but to fear the LORD thy God, to walk in all His ways, and to love Him, and to serve the LORD thy God with all thy heart and with all thy soul." Four things, and they fit in one breath. Revere. Walk in God's ways. Love. Serve. And the next verse adds a fifth: keep the commandments, for your good. Not for God's benefit. For yours. The rabbis couldn't leave the word what alone. The Talmud, in Berakhot, raises an eyebrow: Moses says what does God require, but to fear Him, as if fear of heaven were a small thing. Is it small? The answer given: for Moses, yes. Like someone asked for a large vessel who happens to own one; to him, it seems small. What's simple to state can still take a lifetime to own. And there's a playful reading too. The Hebrew for what is mah. Rabbi Meir, in the Talmud, reads it as me'ah, a hundred, and says a person should say a hundred blessings every day. So the simplest question in the book becomes a hundred small moments of noticing: waking, washing, eating, seeing something beautiful. A prophet centuries later, Micah, asks almost the same question and answers it with justice, mercy, and walking humbly. Two answers, one shape. What is asked is simple to say. The doing is daily.

Eikev. Because, and heel. The portion where Moses boils a whole Torah down to one plain question.

495.title: Eikev: open the heart (Deuteronomy 10:16)
495.hook: "circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked"
495.howItsDone: Some Jewish teachers read this verse together with Deuteronomy 30:6 and the Talmud's teaching that the broken tablets were kept in the ark, as images of repentance, especially in the weeks leading up to the High Holy Days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eikev's plain question: what does God require? Your line was what is asked is simple. Today, a startling picture of a closed heart.

Chapter ten opens in the aftermath of the golden calf. Moses has just recalled the first tablets, thrown down and broken before the people's eyes. Then God tells him: carve two new tablets like the first, and come back up. He does. And the rabbis add a detail the Torah only hints at. In the Talmud they teach that the broken pieces weren't thrown away. They were placed in the ark, beside the whole tablets. A few verses later, Moses tells the people what has to change in them so it doesn't happen again.
screen: `THE TABLETS SHATTERED.` → `CARVE TWO NEW ONES.` → `THE BROKEN PIECES KEPT.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart, and be no more stiffnecked." It's a jarring image, and it's meant to be. The Hebrew word is orlah, and readers hear in it a covering, something that closes over and blocks. The Bible uses the same root for other blocked organs. Back in Exodus, Moses called himself a man of uncircumcised lips, his mouth closed, he felt, to speech. The prophet Jeremiah speaks of ears that are uncircumcised, that can't hear. So an uncircumcised heart is a heart with a layer over it. It knows things, but they don't get in. Then the second half: be no more stiffnecked. The picture, as some readers take it, comes from the farm: an ox that stiffens its neck won't turn where the driver leads. And it echoes what God called the people at the golden calf: a stiffnecked people. So Moses is naming the old problem in two pictures. A covered heart doesn't let anything in. A stiff neck won't turn toward anything. Notice who's asked to do the opening. Here, it's the people: you circumcise your heart. Later in Deuteronomy, in chapter thirty, the same image comes back, and this time it's God who promises to do it for them. Commentators hold both: the opening is your work, and it's also a gift. The broken tablets in the ark make the same point. What cracked can be carried. A heart can be opened again.

segments.voice: Let your shoulders drop and notice your neck, the actual muscles, and let it loosen a little. Bring to mind one person you've closed over; you don't have to forgive anything, only notice the layer. Hold one true thing about them for a few breaths, and let your neck turn toward them, just slightly.
Eikev. Because, and heel. The portion where new tablets are carved, the broken ones kept, and a covered heart is told to open.
Your line: open the heart. A stiff neck can learn to turn. That's day four hundred ninety-five.

496.title: Eikev: love the stranger (Deuteronomy 10:19)
496.hook: "Love ye therefore the stranger; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt"
496.howItsDone: Jewish communities cite the command to love the stranger in teaching about welcoming converts and newcomers, and some Jewish organizations that work with refugees and immigrants cite these verses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eikev's covered heart and stiff neck. Your line was open the heart. Today, the last stop in Eikev, and the person at the edge of the room.

The first week somewhere new. A new school, a new job, a new country. Not knowing where the bathroom is, or which jokes are safe, or whether anyone will sit with you at lunch. Everyone else moves easily through rules you can't see. A year later, that feeling is easy to lose. You become one of the ones who know where everything is. The Torah, it seems, is worried about exactly that forgetting, because it comes back to this person, the stranger, again and again.
screen: `YOUR FIRST WEEK SOMEWHERE NEW.` → `RULES YOU COULDN'T SEE.` → `WE FORGET THE FEELING.`

segments.voice: Moses has just described God as great and mighty, the one who can't be bribed. And then, of all the things to say next: "He doth execute justice for the fatherless and widow, and loveth the stranger, in giving him food and raiment." The God of everything is described by who God feeds and clothes. And the next verse turns it into a command: "Love ye therefore the stranger; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The Hebrew word is ger. In the Torah, a ger is someone living among a people not their own: a resident foreigner, without land, without family nearby, easy to cheat. Later, in rabbinic Hebrew, ger also came to mean a convert, someone who joins the Jewish people, and the rabbis read some of these verses about converts too. Both meanings are about someone arriving from outside. The reason given isn't an argument. It's a memory. You were strangers. In Exodus it's said even more sharply: "for ye know the heart of a stranger." The people Moses speaks to didn't have to imagine it. Their families had lived it, in Egypt. And the Torah keeps coming back to it. The path met this count earlier in the year: the Talmud, in Bava Metzia, says the Torah warns about the stranger in thirty-six places, and some say forty-six. One way to hear the repetition: the command isn't complicated. It's just easy to forget once you're the one who knows where everything is.

Eikev. Because, and heel. The portion that ends its teaching with the stranger, because you were strangers once.

497.title: Re'eh: see the choice (Deuteronomy 11:26)
497.hook: "Behold, I set before you this day a blessing and a curse"
497.howItsDone: Re'eh is read in synagogues in late summer, usually around the start of the month of Elul, when the season of reflection and self-examination before the High Holy Days begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eikev's ger, the stranger, loved because you were strangers once. Your line was love the stranger. Today a new portion opens with one word: look.

Some of the choices that shape a life don't feel like choices while they're being made. Nobody decides to stop calling a brother. It just slowly happens. Nobody chooses two hours of scrolling. They just don't choose not to. Psychologists have names for it: defaults, habits, autopilot. Life comes at you as a stream, and the forks in the road go by without signs. The new portion opens by stopping that stream. Before it says a word about what to choose, it tells you to look.
screen: `CHOICES THAT DON'T FEEL LIKE CHOICES.` → `AUTOPILOT.` → `FIRST, LOOK.`

segments.voice: In the old Jewish translation: "Behold, I set before you this day a blessing and a curse." The first word, behold, is re'eh in Hebrew. See. It gives the portion its name. And there's a small oddity some commentators point out. Re'eh is singular: see, you, one person. But before you is plural: all of you. A whole people stands there, and each one is told to see for themselves. Nobody can look for you. Then the choice is laid out plainly. The blessing, if you listen to the commandments; the curse, if you turn aside. And Moses gives it a geography. When you cross the Jordan, set the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal, two real mountains. Later, in the book of Joshua, the people do exactly that: half of them in front of one mountain, half in front of the other, and the blessing and the curse read aloud. A choice you can stand between and see with your eyes. And then two small words: this day. Not once, at Sinai, settled for good. Today, set before you again. Some Jewish teachers hear in it a basic idea: that a person is free, and the road forks every day. The Torah doesn't pretend the choice is easy, or that it's always obvious. It asks for something earlier and simpler. See it. Notice that there's a fork at all.
screen: `RE'EH: SEE.` · `SEE, YOU. BEFORE ALL OF YOU.` · `GERIZIM AND EBAL.` · `THIS DAY, AGAIN.` · then, large: `SEE THE CHOICE.`

segments.voice: Walk through the rest of your day in your mind, hour by hour, and find one fork you'd normally slide past: the first thing you pick up, what you say when you walk in the door, whether you answer that message. Picture the two mountains facing each other right there. You don't have to decide anything; just mark the spot.
Re'eh. See, or behold. Said to one person, in front of everyone: the first word and the name of the portion.
Your line: see the choice. A week that went beyond the letter, lived by more than bread, credited other hands, asked simply, opened the heart, and loved the stranger. See you tomorrow.
